topic: Research: VS Code Agents Guide 2026: The Agent-Native Companion App

key_points: Official VS Code positioning: built-in agents can plan, edit across a project, run commands, and self-correct while the developer focuses on intent and review.
Covers agent session configuration, tailoring agents to a codebase, trust and control, and getting started workflows.
Strong source for canonical terminology and feature explanations, but less comparative or strategic than a blog guide should be.
Release notes for VS Code 1.115 introduce Visual Studio Code Agents as a preview companion app shipping with VS Code Insiders.

Core claims: parallel tasks across repos, isolated worktrees, inline diffs, progress monitoring, feedback, PR creation, and carried-over VS Code customizations including instructions, prompt files, custom agents, MCP servers, hooks, and plugins.
Important limitation: preview-only and currently tied to VS Code Insiders.
Frames VS Code as a unified multi-agent surface for local, background, and cloud agents.
Explains when to use local interactive agents, background agents in worktrees, and cloud autonomous agents.
Notes Claude and Codex support alongside Copilot under Copilot subscriptions, plus Agent Sessions as the control center.
Compares true VS Code extensions with standalone VS Code forks such as Cursor and Windsurf.
Defines 2026 coding agents by full-codebase context, multi-file edits, terminal execution, MCP integration, and iteration until completion.
Useful competitive angle: developers who want to keep stock VS Code should evaluate extension-native agents differently from agent-native IDE forks.
Hands-on coverage of the VS Code Agents preview, emphasizing the companion-app model rather than another chat panel.
Highlights multi-repo parallelization, isolated worktrees, inline diffs, feedback loops, PR creation, and carried-over customizations.
Useful for practical expectations: still a rapidly evolving preview, not yet a stable default workflow for every team.

stats.fact: Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey reported that 84% of respondents use or plan to use AI tools in development, up from 76% the prior year, and 51% of professional developers use AI tools daily.
GitHub's Octoverse 2025 reported more than 1.1 million public repositories using an LLM SDK, with 693,867 created in the prior 12 months, a 178% year-over-year increase.
GitHub Octoverse reported 518.7 million merged pull requests in 2025, up 29% year over year, and said 80% of new developers on GitHub use Copilot in their first week.
VS Code 1.115 introduced the VS Code Agents preview companion app with parallel sessions, isolated worktrees, inline diffs, feedback, PR creation, and inherited VS Code customizations.
Microsoft's Build 2026 recap says the GitHub Copilot app technical preview lets Copilot Pro, Pro+, Business, and Enterprise users direct multiple agents in parallel from a single My Work view.

Sonar's 2026 State of Code survey coverage reported that 42% of developers' code is AI-generated, expected to reach 65% by 2027, while 96% do not fully trust AI-generated code and only 48% always check it before committing.

The Pragmatic Engineer's 2026 AI tooling survey analysis reported Claude Code as the most-loved tool at 46%, ahead of Cursor at 19% and GitHub Copilot at 9%, while large enterprises tend to default to GitHub Copilot.

The Verge reported in 2026 that GitHub Agent HQ adds Claude and OpenAI Codex agents to GitHub, GitHub Mobile, and VS Code for Copilot Pro Plus and Enterprise users, with more agent integrations planned.

angles: VS Code is moving from editor-plus-chat to an agent control plane: sessions, worktrees, diffs, PRs, and review are becoming first-class UI surfaces.
The companion app matters because agent work is no longer a single sidebar conversation; it is parallel, interruptible, reviewable work across repos.
The practical buyer question is not 'Copilot or Cursor?' but 'stock VS Code extension workflow, VS Code Agents companion app, GitHub Copilot app, or a VS Code fork?'
Isolated worktrees are the hidden infrastructure feature: they let teams run several agents without corrupting the main workspace or mixing diffs.
Custom agents and handoffs turn VS Code into a role-based workflow system: planner, implementer, reviewer, security checker, test writer.
MCP, hooks, prompt files, custom instructions, and skills are now part of developer-tool portability; teams should document agent setup the same way they document devcontainers.
Trust and governance are the differentiator for teams: permissions, review checkpoints, terminal approvals, model policies, and code attribution matter more as agent autonomy rises.
Agent-native does not mean developer-absent; the winning workflow is intent, scoped delegation, live monitoring, review, tests, and explicit merge control.
